topics: 📍 Where Do the Inner Altar's Ashes Go? — a verse originally about the bird burnt offering, reapplied
🕊️ Rabbi Shimon vs. the Rabbis — are premature doves subject to me'ilah, and why the difference from an animal too young?
💀 Ulla's Rule on Offerings That Died — Rav Ḥisda's two sharp challenges
🩸 Why Blood Carries Torah-Level Me'ilah But Milk and Dung Do Not
🥚 New Mishna: Milk and Eggs of Consecrated Animals — the difference between altar-bound and Temple-maintenance consecration

overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Ashes to Blood to Milk
overview.subtitle: Meilah 12a–12b
overview.hebrewSource: קָדָשִׁים שֶׁמֵּתוּ, יָצְאוּ מִידֵי מְעִילָה דְּבַר תּוֹרָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by tracing the verse that places the inner altar's ashes and the menorah's wicks in the same disposal spot as the outer altar's ashes. A new mishna records Rabbi Shimon's dissent: unlike the Rabbis, he holds that doves too young for sacrifice ARE subject to me'ilah, paralleling his view that consecrating an item before its proper time creates only a prohibition, not karet. The Gemara then returns to Ulla's rule that sacrificial animals which died lose Torah-level me'ilah, defended by Ulla against two sharp challenges from Rav Ḥisda — the second of which forces a close look at why blood, unlike milk or dung, is understood to be part of the animal's very body. The daf closes with a new mishna distinguishing an animal consecrated for the altar from one consecrated only for its monetary value.

slides.title: 📍 Tracing the Verse for the Inner Altar's Ashes
slides.subtitle: Reapplying a phrase originally about the bird burnt offering

nodes.content: ❓ The outer altar's ashes are placed 'beside the altar' (Lev. 6:3) — but where do the INNER altar's ashes go?
📜 Rabbi Elazar: the phrase 'in the place of the ashes' (Lev. 1:16, about the bird burnt offering) is otherwise unnecessary — apply it to the inner altar
🤔 Challenge: maybe both verses just describe the OUTER altar, fixing its precise location?
✅ Rejected: if so, the verse would say 'beside the altar' plainly — the extra words 'the place of the ashes' teach a NEW location, the inner altar
🕯️ Menorah wicks join the list too — from the definite article 'the ashes' (הַדָּשֶׁן) instead of plain 'ashes'

slides.title: 🕊️ Are Premature Doves Subject to Me'ilah?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon breaks from the Rabbis' view

lines.speaker: Rabbi Shimon
lines.text: Doves too young for sacrifice ARE subject to me'ilah. Pigeons too old are only forbidden ab initio, not subject to me'ilah — consistent with my general rule: consecrating something before its proper time creates only a prohibition, never karet.

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: Neither premature doves nor overage pigeons are subject to me'ilah at all — merely forbidden ab initio.

lines.speaker: Question for Rabbis
lines.text: But an animal too young (מְחוּסַּר זְמַן) CAN still be consecrated and enters the tithing pen with others — why are premature birds different?

lines.speaker: Rabbis' answer
lines.text: A young or blemished animal is always redeemable, so its consecration takes hold at least for value. Birds have no concept of blemish-disqualification, so premature birds have no redemption option at all — their 'consecration' never really takes hold.

slides.title: 💀 Ulla's Rule, Challenged Twice by Rav Ḥisda
slides.subtitle: Do sacrificial animals that died lose Torah-level me'ilah — and where did their sanctity go?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Ulla (citing R' Yoḥanan): sacrificial animals that died are excluded from me'ilah BY TORAH LAW — they can't be sacrificed or even redeemed (not to feed dogs)

2️⃣ Rav Ḥisda's first challenge: 'Where did their sanctity GO?' Ulla counters: the mishna itself says the same about premature/overage birds — so both must mean 'no Torah-level me'ilah, but rabbinic me'ilah remains'

3️⃣ Rav Ḥisda concedes that point, but raises a second challenge: is there any precedent for something that starts WITHOUT me'ilah and later gains it (like these birds gaining only rabbinic me'ilah)? What about blood — no me'ilah before sprinkling, me'ilah after reaching the Kidron?

4️⃣ Resolution: blood is NOT a real precedent — it actually has TORAH-LEVEL me'ilah from the very start, since one who lets blood from a LIVE sacrificial animal is already liable for misuse by Torah law

slides.title: 🩸 Blood vs. Milk vs. Dung: Why the Different Rules?
slides.subtitle: What counts as truly 'part of' a consecrated animal's body?

boxes.title: Blood
items: The animal CANNOT exist without blood
Subject to me'ilah even while the animal is alive (Torah law)
Considered inseparable from the animal itself

boxes.title: Milk
items: The animal CAN exist without milk
NOT subject to me'ilah — forbidden to benefit from ab initio only
Treated as a distinct byproduct, not the animal's essence

boxes.title: Dung / Manure
items: Continuously replaced — old food leaves, new food enters
NOT subject to me'ilah — forbidden ab initio only
Its money goes to the treasury chamber (Rabbi Elazar's rule for 'consecrated and not consecrated' items)

slides.title: 🥚 New Mishna: Milk and Eggs — Two Kinds of Consecration
slides.subtitle: Everything depends on whether the animal itself was meant for the altar or only for its value
rows: Kedushat haguf for the altar (e.g. an animal meant to be sacrificed)
NOT subject to me'ilah — no benefit ab initio, but no liability after
Kedushat damim for the altar (consecrated to be SOLD, proceeds buying an offering)
Subject to me'ilah, treated like Temple-maintenance property
Subject to me'ilah (Rav Pappa's clarification) — animal and byproduct are one unit
Consecrated for Temple maintenance (bedek habayit) — e.g. a hen or donkey
Subject to me'ilah — animal and byproduct are one unit

callout.label: Rav Pappa's fix:
callout.text: The mishna's wording is incomplete: an animal consecrated with inherent sanctity FOR THE ALTAR keeps its milk/eggs separate from me'ilah; but once consecration is only for value (kedushat damim) — even if ultimately destined for the altar — it's treated just like Temple-maintenance property, where the animal and its produce form a single consecrated unit.

summary.principle: Me'ilah tracks what is truly part of a consecrated body versus what is separable from it — blood, inseparable from a living animal, carries Torah-level me'ilah from the start, while milk, eggs, and dung remain outside me'ilah unless the underlying consecration is for value rather than for the altar itself.

🕊️ R' Shimon vs. Rabbis: premature doves — me'ilah or not?

columns.content: 💀 Dead sacrificial animals: no Torah-level me'ilah, but rabbinic me'ilah remains
🩸 Blood: Torah-level me'ilah from the moment it's drawn from a living animal

flowSteps.content: 🥚 Milk and eggs of altar-bound animals: no me'ilah; of value-consecrated or Temple-maintenance animals: full me'ilah
🎓 Key Principle: me'ilah follows what is inseparable from a consecrated body, not merely what originates from it

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Elazar, how is the location for burying the inner altar's ashes derived from the Torah?
o: It is not derived at all; it's a purely rabbinic enactment
From the phrase 'in the place of the ashes' in the verse about the bird burnt offering (Lev. 1:16), which would otherwise be unnecessary
From a direct verse naming the inner altar specifically
From an oral tradition with no scriptural basis
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar reasons that since the phrase is unnecessary for the outer altar (already taught elsewhere), it must be teaching a new halakha — that the inner altar's ashes go to the same place.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Shimon hold that doves too young for sacrifice ARE subject to me'ilah, unlike the Rabbis' view?
o: Because he holds all birds are always subject to me'ilah
Because it fits his general principle that consecrating an item before its proper time creates only a prohibition (not karet), implying the consecration itself does take effect
Because young doves are worth more money
Because he disagrees with the entire concept of me'ilah
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon's broader position is that early consecration is effective (creating a prohibition), which is consistent with holding that premature doves retain consecrated status and are subject to me'ilah.

quiz.q: How does Ulla resolve Rav Ḥisda's second challenge — that blood seems to be a precedent for something starting without me'ilah and later acquiring it, contradicting the birds' rabbinic-only me'ilah?
o: He admits defeat and retracts his opinion
He points out that blood actually has Torah-level me'ilah from the start, since letting blood from a living sacrificial animal is already forbidden and subject to misuse by Torah law
He says blood is never subject to me'ilah at any point
He says the challenge is irrelevant to his original rule
quiz.e: Ulla (or the Gemara on his behalf) explains that blood is not a true precedent, since it already carries Torah-level me'ilah while the animal is alive — unlike the birds, whose initial state truly lacks any me'ilah.

quiz.q: Why is blood subject to me'ilah while milk is not, according to Rav's explanation to Rav Hamnuna?
o: Because milk is never consumed by anyone
Because the animal cannot exist without blood, making it part of the animal itself, while the animal can exist without milk
Because blood is more valuable than milk
Because milk belongs exclusively to the owner, not the Temple
quiz.e: Rav explains that blood is inseparable from the animal's existence, so it shares the animal's consecrated status, whereas milk is a separable byproduct the animal can live without.

quiz.q: According to Rav Pappa's clarification of the new mishna, when ARE the milk and eggs of a consecrated animal subject to me'ilah?
o: Never, under any circumstances
Only when the animal was consecrated with inherent sanctity (kedushat haguf) specifically for the altar
When the animal was consecrated with sanctity that inheres in its value (kedushat damim) for the altar, or for Temple maintenance — in both cases treated as one unit with the animal
Only for donkeys, never for hens
quiz.e: Rav Pappa explains that milk/eggs escape me'ilah only when the animal itself was consecrated with inherent sanctity for direct sacrifice; when consecrated for its value or for Temple maintenance, the animal and its produce are treated as a single consecrated unit, both subject to me'ilah.
